newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Schengen pact expands to Nordic countries.
newsitem.headline: Schengen pact expands to Nordic countries.

text.p: The Schengen agreement -- Europe's most ambitious border-free pact yet -- spread its wings on Thursday to the five countries of the Nordic Passport Union.

But the signing of accession pacts by the 10-nation group with EU members Denmark, Sweden and Finland and cooperation accords with non-EU members Norway and Iceland will not have an immediate impact on travellers.
"It's a determining moment in the history of Schengen," Luxembourg's Justice Minister Marc Fischbach said at the signing held during a meeting of the organisation's executive.
"The Schengen space will now stretch as far as the eastern frontier of Finland to the Atlantic and the Mediterranean."

He admitted that it could take until the year 1999 or 2000 for the benefits to show for travellers from other Schengen countries -- Austria, France, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece.
Under the pact seven of the Schengen members dropped airport passport checks with each other in March 1995 and were supposed to drop land border checks on July 1, 1995.
But an underpinning principle of Schengen is that passport controls should only be dropped when adequate safeguards are in place to prevent the zone becoming a playground for organised crime.

A recent spate of guerrilla bombings in France seemed to make it even more unlikely that France -- which has refused for more than a year to honour a commitment to drop land border controls with its neighbours Belgium and Luxembourg -- would have a change heart.
Officials said French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier, who outlined measures taken to deal with the attacks, had not shown any movement.
France has stalled on removing land-border checks with the two countries, accusing them of being transit points for drugs coming from the Netherlands, with which it is at loggerheads on drugs policy.

Three of the existing 10 Schengen members -- Austria, Italy and Greece -- do not yet fully apply the deal although they hope to do so by October provided room can be found in the overloaded Schengen computer system.

For the same reason, the new Nordic countries might not actually apply the deal until 1999 or 2000, Fischbach said. "We hope that by the latest -- 1999 or 2000 -- the five countries will be definitively integrated."
It was agreed on Thursday, he said, to study how a second computer could be set up to help the first correlate data from national police forces linked in the cross-border fight against crime.
Fischbach said the computer had already helped find some wanted people and stolen cars.

Norwegian Secretary of State for Justice and Police, Oeystein Maeland, whose country voted against joining the European Union, said it was cooperating with Schengen to preserve the 40-year-old Nordic Passport Union and fight organised crime.
"We will better contribute and also gain in the fight against international organised crime," he said.
